english: as much as / to the same degree as (N)
formNote: 만큼 attaches straight onto a noun with no space and no sound change (너→너만큼, 형→형만큼, 돈→돈만큼) and sets that noun as the yardstick: 'as Adj as N.' It also rides on a verb/adjective modifier — 먹은 만큼 (as much as you ate), 노력한 만큼 (as much as you tried) — but THERE 만큼 is spaced and means 'in proportion to,' which is the dividing line learners blur: glued to a bare noun = equal degree, spaced after -은/는/을 = proportional payoff. Compare it with 처럼: 만큼 measures AMOUNT/degree ('as much as'), while 처럼 measures MANNER/likeness ('like, in the way of'), so 너처럼 means 'like you (in style)' but 너만큼 means 'to the same level as you.' The big English-speaker trap is that 만큼 has no separate word for 'as'; you do NOT add a second 'as,' and the adjective comes LAST: 너만큼 잘해 (literally 'you-as-much do-well'), never 만큼 잘해 너.
usage: I want to be as good as you
Bare noun as the standard of comparison
It's not as expensive as I thought
생각만큼 = as much as expected; very common with negatives
You get out as much as you put in
I love you as much as the sky
Noun as a vivid yardstick of degree
examples: 나도 너만큼 키 컸으면 좋겠다.
I wish I were as tall as you.
Simple equal-degree comparison off a bare noun (너만큼)
솔직히 월급만큼만 일하면 됐죠 뭐.
Honestly, working just as much as my paycheck is plenty, right?
월급만큼만 stacks 만 = 'exactly as much as, no more'; relatable work attitude
기대한 만큼 재미있진 않았는데 볼 만은 했어요.
It wasn't as fun as I'd hoped, but it was watchable.
Real verdict: spaced 기대한 만큼 = proportional to expectation, then a softening 볼 만은
mistakes: Adding a leftover 'as' or fronting the adjective: English 'as good as you' tempts 만큼 잘해 너, but Korean keeps the order 너만큼 잘해 — the standard (너만큼) comes first, the predicate last, with no second 'as.'
Spacing it off a plain noun: write 너만큼 / 돈만큼 as one word, never 너 만큼. The space appears ONLY after a verb/adjective modifier: 한 만큼, 먹은 만큼.
Confusing 만큼 with 처럼. 'Cried like a child' (manner) is 아이처럼 울었어요, not 아이만큼 울었어요 — 만큼 would mean 'cried to the same QUANTITY as a child,' which is not the intended 'in the manner of.'

english: considering it's (an) N / for an N (it's surprisingly...)
formNote: 치고 glues to a noun with no space (초보→초보치고, 겨울→겨울치고) and means 'measured against the norm for an N, this defies that norm' — i.e. better/worse/different than an N usually is. Add 는 → 치고는 to lean harder into the contrast (주말치고는 한산해요). The closest cousin is N에 비해 ('compared to'), but the line is sharp: 에 비해 lines up two separate things ('A에 비해 B' = relative to A, B is...), whereas 치고 stays inside ONE category and plays the member off its own stereotype ('for a beginner, surprisingly good'). There's also a flipped use — N치고 + a negative = 'there's no N that isn't...': 한국 사람치고 김치 안 먹는 사람 없어요 ('no Korean doesn't eat kimchi'); context separates the two instantly. English-speaker pitfall: don't reach for 치다 (to hit) — this 치고 is a fixed comparative particle, and learners wrongly try to translate 'for' with 위해 (which means 'for the sake of,' a totally different 'for').
usage: Core 'better than the norm for an N'
치고 + a description that breaks the stereotype
치고는 stresses the contrast more strongly
한국 사람치고 매운 거 못 먹는 사람 없어요
There's no Korean who can't eat spicy food
examples: 이 식당 가격치고 양 많네요.
For the price, this place gives a big portion.
Simple shopping verdict; 가격치고 plays cost off the expected portion
월요일치고는 도로가 안 막히네요.
For a Monday, the roads aren't that jammed.
치고는 leans into the surprise; everyday commute small talk
걔 신입치고 일 진짜 잘하던데, 경력직인 줄 알았어.
He's seriously good for a new hire — I thought he was experienced.
Real workplace praise; 신입치고 contrasts a rookie with veteran-level work
mistakes: Translating 'for' with 위해: 'good for a beginner' is 초보치고 잘해요, NOT 초보를 위해 잘해요 (that means 'does well for the beginner's sake'). 치고 is the comparative 'for,' 위해 is the benefactive 'for.'
Spacing or swapping for 치다: write 초보치고 as one word, never 초보 치고, and don't think of the verb 치다 (to hit) — here 치고 is a frozen particle of comparison.
Forcing 에 비해 where 치고 fits: 'good for a beginner' is one category judged against its own norm → 초보치고; 에 비해 would demand a separate yardstick (프로에 비해 = compared to a pro), changing the meaning.

english: looks / seems (a certain way) — judging by appearance
formNote: Take an adjective's -아/어 form and add 보이다 (spaced): ㅏ/ㅗ stems take -아 보이다 (좋다→좋아 보이다, 작다→작아 보이다), others take -어 보이다 (힘들다→힘들어 보이다), 하다 adjectives → 해 보이다 (피곤하다→피곤해 보이다), and ㅡ-stems drop the ㅡ (예쁘다→예뻐 보이다, 바쁘다→바빠 보이다). The whole point is JUDGING BY SIGHT — 보이다 is the passive/intransitive of 보다 ('to see'), so it literally says 'X shows up as Adj to the eye.' The crucial contrast is with -(으)ㄴ/는 것 같다 ('seems'): 것 같다 covers ANY evidence — texts, tone, a hunch — while 아/어 보이다 is reserved for what you actually SEE, which is the exact pitfall: 'he seems busy (from his messages)' must be 바쁜 것 같아요, not 바빠 보여요. Also keep -아/어 보이다 (looks) apart from the identical-looking -아/어 보다 ('try doing'); only adjectives + 보이다 give the 'appears' meaning, while verbs + 보다 give 'attempt.'
usage: Reading someone's face — the everyday use
어리다 → 어려 보이다; a common compliment
Judging an item purely by sight
You look like you're in a good mood
좋다 → 좋아 보이다; appearance reveals a mood
examples: 그 가방 진짜 비싸 보인다.
That bag really looks expensive.
Simple sight-based judgment; ㅏ-stem 비싸 + 보이다
오늘따라 좀 안 좋아 보이는데 무슨 일 있어요?
You look a bit off today — is something wrong?
오늘따라 = today of all days; a caring, appearance-prompted check-in
이거 입으니까 한 살은 어려 보이지 않아?
Don't I look a year younger in this?
Real fitting-room moment; 어려 보이다 is the go-to beauty phrase
mistakes: Using it for non-visual guesses: 'It seems he's busy (judging by his texts)' is 바쁜 것 같아요, not 바빠 보여요 — 보이다 needs something you can literally SEE.
Mixing it up with -아/어 보다 (try): 입어 보다 means 'try wearing,' while 좋아 보이다 means 'looks good.' Verbs + 보다 = attempt; adjectives + 보이다 = appearance.
Forgetting the ㅡ-drop: 예쁘다 becomes 예뻐 보여요, not 예쁘어 보여요, and 바쁘다 → 바빠 보여요, not 바쁘어 보여요.

formNote: 에 비해 attaches to a noun (작년→작년에 비해, 가격→가격에 비해) and frames 'relative to N, this is more/less...' 비해 is the -아/어 form of the Sino-Korean verb 비하다 (比하다, 比 'compare'); fuller variants are 에 비해서 (서 added, conversational) and the written/formal 에 비하여. To compare against a clause, nominalize first: V-는 것에 비해 (사는 것에 비해 = compared to living...). It overlaps with N치고 but differs sharply: 에 비해 lines up TWO separate items as a measuring stick ('A에 비해 B'), while 치고 keeps one item inside its own category ('for an N'). English-speaker pitfalls cluster here: (1) the particle is 에, not 와/하고, so 'compared TO last year' is 작년에 비해, never 작년과 비해 or 작년 비해; (2) don't substitute the everyday verb 비교하다 (比較하다, 'to compare') — the set adverbial phrase is locked as 비하다→비해, so 가격과 비교해서 is grammatical as a full verb but is NOT this fixed pattern.
usage: It's expensive compared to last year
Comparing the same thing across time
가격에 비해 = relative to the price
You look young for your age
Your Korean has improved a lot compared to before
examples: 이건 저것에 비해 좀 작아요.
This is a bit smaller compared to that one.
Simple side-by-side of two items with 에 비해
서울은 지방에 비해 월세가 훨씬 비싸요.
Rent in Seoul is way higher compared to outside the capital.
지방 = the provinces; 월세 = monthly rent; everyday cost-of-living talk
연차에 비해 연봉이 좀 짠 편이라 이직 고민 중이에요.
My salary's a bit stingy for my years in, so I'm weighing a job change.
연차 = years of experience, 연봉 = annual salary, 짜다 = stingy; real career gripe
mistakes: Using the wrong particle: it's N에 비해, not N과/와 비해 or bare N 비해. 'Compared to last year' = 작년에 비해.
Swapping in 비교해(서): the fixed phrase is 비하다 → 비해. 비교하다 is a normal verb ('가격을 비교해 봤어요' = I compared the prices), but it is not this set 에 비해 pattern.
Trying to attach it straight to a verb: you can't say 사는 에 비해. Nominalize first — 사는 것에 비해 (compared to living/buying).

english: even though / despite the fact that
formNote: This is the -는데/-(으)ㄴ데 background ending plus 도 ('even'), literally 'even given the situation that...' Present verbs take -는데도 (먹다→먹는데도, 하다→하는데도); adjectives take -(으)ㄴ데도 (춥다→추운데도, 바쁘다→바쁜데도); the past for both is -았/었는데도 (잤는데도 = even though I slept); nouns take N인데도. It means 'even though X (which I'd expect to lead elsewhere), surprisingly Y.' The sharp contrast is with plain -지만 ('but'): -지만 is a flat, neutral 'but' that just joins two facts, whereas -는데도 carries the speaker's surprise or frustration that the expected consequence FAILED to follow (열심히 했지만 떨어졌어요 = 'I worked hard but failed,' a calm statement; 열심히 했는데도 떨어졌어요 = 'I worked hard and STILL failed?!', with felt letdown). English-speaker pitfall: the 'still/anyway' that English often adds in the second clause is already baked into -는데도, and the most common error is picking the wrong modifier — adjectives never take -는데도.
usage: Even though I worked hard, I failed
Even though it's cold, I (still) go out
Even though I ate, I'm hungry
Even though I'm broke, I bought it again
examples: 비싼데도 사람이 많아요.
Even though it's expensive, it's crowded.
Simple adjective form 비싼데도; the result defies the price
야근 많이 했는데도 월급은 그대로네요.
Even after all the overtime, my salary's the same.
야근 = overtime; the resigned 그대로네요 carries the frustration -는데도 implies
분명히 알람 맞춰 놨는데도 또 늦잠 잤어.
I clearly set an alarm and still overslept again.
늦잠 자다 = oversleep; 분명히 + -는데도 amplifies the 'and yet?!' feeling
mistakes: Putting adjectives in the verb form: it's 추운데도 / 바쁜데도, not 춥는데도 / 바쁘는데도. Present VERBS use -는데도; ADJECTIVES use -(으)ㄴ데도.
Choosing flat -지만 when you mean frustrated surprise: '열심히 했지만 떨어졌어요' just reports two facts, while '열심히 했는데도 떨어졌어요' conveys 'and yet I STILL failed.' Use -는데도 when the expected outcome didn't follow.
Adding a redundant 'still': you don't need a separate word for 'still/anyway' — it's already inside -는데도, so 밥 먹었는데도 배고파요 already means 'even though I ate, I'm STILL hungry.'

english: only / merely (do) — nothing more than that
formNote: Attach -ㄹ 뿐이다 to vowel-ending stems (하다→할 뿐이다) and -을 뿐이다 to consonant stems (믿다→믿을 뿐이다); 뿐 is a bound noun, so it is spaced from the modifier. The past is -았/었을 뿐이다 (도와줬을 뿐이에요 = I only helped), and a noun takes N일 뿐이다 (친구일 뿐이에요). It pins the situation down to exactly ONE thing — 'that's all there is to it' — and is frequently defensive or modest. Watch the close rival 만 ('only'): 만 narrows the noun/object ('나만 = only ME'), but -(으)ㄹ 뿐이다 narrows the whole PREDICATE/action ('I only DID, nothing else'), and the two even team up as -(으)ㄹ 뿐 (just) for emphasis. The flagship English-speaker pitfall is confusing -(으)ㄹ 뿐이다 with -(으)ㄹ 뿐만 아니라: the first CLOSES a statement off ('merely that and no more'), while the second OPENS it up ('not only that, but also'). They look almost identical but point in opposite directions.
usage: Limiting your action to one thing
Modest set phrase, very common in interviews
Noun → N일 뿐이에요; clearing up assumptions
examples: 저는 그냥 듣고 있을 뿐이에요.
I'm just listening, that's all.
Simple 'nothing more than this one action' with 있을 뿐이에요
좋아하는 게 아니라 그냥 친한 동기일 뿐이야.
It's not that I like him, he's just a close peer.
동기 = same-cohort coworker/classmate; the noun form N일 뿐 clears up gossip
불평하는 게 아니라 사실을 말할 뿐이에요.
I'm not complaining, I'm only stating a fact.
A standard way to soften a blunt remark — 'A가 아니라 B할 뿐'
mistakes: Confusing it with 뿐만 아니라: -(으)ㄹ 뿐이다 CLOSES things off ('only that'), but -(으)ㄹ 뿐만 아니라 OPENS them up ('not only that, but also'). Mixing them flips your meaning.
Gluing 뿐 to the verb: 뿐 is a bound noun and must be spaced — 할 뿐이에요, not 할뿐이에요. (After a NOUN, though, 뿐 attaches: 친구일 뿐.)
Dropping the modifier: it's -(으)ㄹ 뿐이다, not the bare stem — say 믿을 뿐이에요, not 믿 뿐이에요.

formNote: Attach -ㄹ 뿐만 아니라 to vowel stems (싸다→쌀 뿐만 아니라) and -을 뿐만 아니라 to consonant stems (좋다→좋을 뿐만 아니라); the past is -았/었을 뿐만 아니라. Literally it's 뿐 ('only') + 만 ('just') + 아니라 ('and not'), i.e. 'it isn't JUST that...,' so the second clause piles on something MORE, typically marked with 도 ('also'): 'not only A, but B too.' The handiest shape is the noun form N뿐만 아니라 (돈뿐만 아니라 = not only money), where 뿐만 glues onto the noun. The near-twin is -(으)ㄹ 뿐이다, which does the OPPOSITE — it shuts a statement down to one thing, while 뿐만 아니라 adds a second; one closes, one opens. A second useful contrast is N뿐만 아니라 vs N도 ('also'): 도 just tags one extra item, whereas 뿐만 아니라 explicitly says 'even beyond the obvious first thing.' English-speaker pitfall: don't separate the noun with a space (it's 돈뿐만, not 돈 뿐만), and remember the pairing 'not only A but also B' is realized with a trailing 도 in clause two, not a fronted word for 'also.'
usage: It's not only tasty but also cheap
Two pluses stacked on a verb/adjective stem
Not just me — everyone's like that
I not only work but also study
It's not only in Seoul but also in the provinces
examples: 이거 싸뿐만 아니라 맛도 좋아.
This is not only cheap but also tastes good.
Simple two-virtue stack; clause two takes 맛도 with 도
이 집은 가성비 좋을 뿐만 아니라 사장님도 친절해요.
This place isn't just good value — the owner's friendly too.
가성비 = value for money; restaurant rec where 도 carries the second plus
요즘 물가는 월세뿐만 아니라 식비까지 다 올랐어요.
Lately prices have risen for not just rent but food too.
물가 = cost of living, 식비 = food expenses; the noun form with 까지 intensifying
mistakes: Confusing it with -(으)ㄹ 뿐이다: 뿐만 아니라 ADDS a second thing ('not only... but also'), while 뿐이다 LIMITS to one ('merely'). They look alike but do opposite jobs.
Spacing the noun form: it's 돈뿐만 아니라 (뿐만 glues to the noun), with a space only before 아니라. Don't write 돈 뿐만 아니라.
Dropping the 도 in the second clause: 'not only A but also B' lands as ...뿐만 아니라 B도..., e.g. 일할 뿐만 아니라 공부도 해요, not 일할 뿐만 아니라 공부 해요.

english: in order to / for the sake of (doing)
formNote: Attach -기 위해(서) to a verb stem (모으다→모으기 위해, 합격하다→합격하기 위해); 위해서 (with 서) is conversational, 위하여 is the formal/written form. 위해 comes from the Sino-Korean verb 위하다 (爲하다, 爲 'for the sake of'). After a noun, use N을/를 위해(서) (가족→가족을 위해 = for my family). It marks a DELIBERATE, planned goal, so it reads a touch more formal and purposeful than casual -(으)려고 ('intending to'); that's the sharp contrast — -(으)려고 is everyday spoken intention and dislikes formal endings (-(으)려고 합니다 is fine, but goals on signs/resolutions prefer 위해), while -기 위해 suits written aims, mission statements, and earnest explanations. English-speaker pitfalls: (1) a NOUN needs 을/를 — 건강을 위해, never 건강 위해; (2) a VERB uses the -기 nominalizer, never the dictionary form — 모으기 위해, never 모으다 위해; (3) the subject of both clauses should match (you can't easily use 위해 to say 'so that SOMEONE ELSE does X' — for that, switch to -도록 or -게).
usage: I work part-time to save money
The goal, then the action taken toward it
I study in order to pass
I work hard for my family's sake
examples: 살을 빼기 위해 매일 걸어요.
I walk every day in order to lose weight.
Simple goal + means; verb takes the -기 form (빼기 위해)
전세금 모으기 위해서 진짜 안 쓰고 살고 있어요.
I'm living super frugally to save up for a jeonse deposit.
전세금 = lump-sum housing deposit; 위해서 (with 서) is natural in speech
더 나은 조건을 위해 이직 준비 중이에요.
I'm prepping a job change for better conditions.
이직 = changing jobs; noun + 위해 framing a purposeful plan
mistakes: Omitting 을/를 after a noun: say 건강을 위해, not 건강 위해. The noun pattern is N을/를 위해(서).
Using the dictionary form with a verb: it's the -기 nominalizer — 모으기 위해, not 모으다 위해 or 모아 위해.
Reaching for 위해 to mean 'so that someone ELSE does X': 위해 wants the same subject in both clauses, so 'I cleaned so the kids could play' is better with -게/-도록 (놀 수 있게/놀도록), not 놀기 위해.

english: as long as / so long as (a condition holds)
formNote: Attach -는 한 to a verb stem (살다→사는 한, with ㄹ dropping before ㄴ; 있다→있는 한). This 한 is the Sino-Korean noun 限 ('limit, boundary'), so the clause literally sets 'the boundary/extent within which' the main clause stays true. It very often appears negative — V-지 않는 한 (포기하지 않는 한 = as long as you don't give up) = 'unless.' The sharp contrast is with plain -(으)면 ('if'): -(으)면 is a loose, common 'if/when' that just triggers a result, whereas -는 한 draws a firm CONDITION-BOUNDARY that must hold the whole time ('for as long as / only within the limit that'), so it feels stronger and more absolute — 비가 오면 안 가요 ('if it rains, I won't go') vs 비가 오지 않는 한 가요 ('I'll go unless it rains,' i.e. rain is the one boundary that stops me). English-speaker pitfall: this is a TIME/condition 'as long as,' not the QUANTITY 'as much as' (that's 만큼), and the literary set phrase 가능한 한 ('as far as possible') is fixed — don't read 한 as the number 'one.'
usage: 살다 → 사는 한 (ㄹ drops before ㄴ)
as long as you don't give up, it works
I'll help as much as I can
할 수 있는 한 = within the limit of what's possible
I'll go as soon as possible
가능한 한 = as far as possible (frozen set phrase)
examples: 규칙을 지키는 한 문제없어요.
As long as you follow the rules, there's no problem.
Simple condition-boundary; affirmative 지키는 한
계약서에 사인 안 하는 한 환불 돼요.
As long as you don't sign the contract, you can get a refund.
계약서 = contract; the negative 안 하는 한 = 'unless you sign,' a practical consumer point
특별한 일 없는 한 보통 9시까지 출근해요.
Unless something special comes up, I usually get in by 9.
출근 = go to work; 없는 한 = 'unless there is,' framing the default routine
mistakes: Forgetting the ㄹ-drop: 살다/알다 become 사는 한 / 아는 한 before -는, not 살는 한 / 알는 한.

Swapping in -(으)면 when you need a firm boundary: '비가 오면 안 가요' (if it rains) is softer than '비가 오지 않는 한 가요' (unless it rains). Use -는 한 for a condition that must hold throughout, especially the 'unless' sense.
Confusing this 한 (限, limit/extent) with 만큼: 'as long as I live' (time/condition) is 사는 한, while 'as much as I can' in QUANTITY would be a 만큼 idea — and never read 한 as the number 'one.'

english: so much that... / as a result of being so... (and then something happened)
formNote: Attach the past modifier -(으)ㄴ + 나머지 to verbs and adjectives (놀라다→놀란 나머지, 긴장하다→긴장한 나머지, 기쁘다→기쁜 나머지); consonant stems take -은 나머지 (참다→참은 나머지). 나머지 normally means 'the remainder/leftover,' and here it figuratively names 'what spilled over from an extreme state' — i.e. the first clause was SO intense that it overflowed into the (usually negative or startling) result in the second. The natural rival is -아/어서 ('because'): -아/어서 states a plain, calm cause-and-effect, whereas -(으)ㄴ 나머지 dramatizes an EXTREME degree whose overflow produced an unintended result (긴장해서 실수했어요 = 'I was nervous so I slipped,' neutral; 긴장한 나머지 이름까지 까먹었어요 = 'I was SO nervous I even forgot my name,' vivid and excessive). It's somewhat literary/dramatic, shining in storytelling, news, and lively retellings rather than flat chit-chat. English-speaker pitfall: it ALWAYS takes the past modifier -(으)ㄴ even for a present feeling — never -는 나머지 — and the result clause should be a real, often unwanted consequence, not just any factual statement.
usage: I was so startled that I screamed
Extreme cause overflowing into a result
I was so nervous I stammered
He was so angry he just stormed out
Strong emotion drives an impulsive result
I was so happy that I cried
examples: 너무 기쁜 나머지 눈물이 났어요.
I was so overjoyed that tears came.
Simple emotion-overflow with the adjective form 기쁜 나머지
너무 긴장한 나머지 면접에서 이름까지 까먹었어요.
I was so nervous I even forgot my name in the interview.
면접 = job interview, 까먹다 = forget; the excessive result a dramatic retelling needs
급한 나머지 지갑도 안 챙기고 나왔지 뭐야.
I was in such a rush I left without even my wallet.
급하다 = be in a hurry; casual storytelling capped with -지 뭐야
mistakes: Using the present -는 나머지: this pattern ALWAYS takes the past modifier -(으)ㄴ even for a current feeling — 놀란 나머지, not 놀라는 나머지; 긴장한 나머지, not 긴장하는 나머지.
Choosing it for an everyday, calm cause: for plain 'because' use -아/어서 (긴장해서 실수했어요). Reserve -(으)ㄴ 나머지 for an EXTREME degree that overflows into an unintended/dramatic result.

Pairing it with a neutral, expected outcome: the second clause should be a striking or unwanted consequence (so-much-that...), not a flat fact — 'I was so nervous I forgot my name' fits; 'I was so nervous I prepared well' does not.
